reference_drawer.description: Essential formulas for the empirical relationship between Mean, Median, and Mode.

items.rule: Relationship connecting Mean, Median, and Mode.

items.example: Use when Mode and Median are known.
Use when Mode and Mean are known.

items.rule: Difference form of the empirical relationship.
items.example: A Mode–Median difference of 14 implies Median–Mean difference of 7.

concepts.title: 1. The Empirical Formula
concepts.subtitle: Connect Mean, Median, and Mode
concepts.summary: For a moderately skewed distribution, the empirical relationship connects the three central-tendency measures and allows one measure to be estimated from the other two.

concepts.title: 2. Algebraic Rearrangement
concepts.subtitle: Solve for any one measure
concepts.summary: Rearrange the empirical equation before substituting numbers when Mean, Median, or Mode is the unknown.

concepts.title: 3. Difference Relations
concepts.subtitle: Compare separations between measures
concepts.summary: Subtracting one central-tendency measure from the empirical relation creates useful difference identities.
concepts.trap: Losing the sign when working with signed differences.

concepts.title: 4. Contextual Estimation
concepts.subtitle: Apply the relationship to calculated measures
concepts.summary: When a real-world dataset provides Mean and Median, the empirical relationship can be used to estimate Mode while preserving the context and units.

points.text: Map calculated values to Mean and Median.

concepts.trap: Treating the empirical estimate as an exact universal identity.
